findings.statement: REFUTED: the new per-(run, agent_id) flock lock in subagent_stop_validate.py (acquire_agent_lock / consume_under_agent_lock) does not wedge any legitimate flow I could construct. Cross-run reuse of one agent_id (different runs, different admissions/<run>/.agent-locks/ trees) is unaffected -- confirmed via the shipped test_one_agent_bound_in_one_run_is_still_admissible_in_another, which passes. Same-agent re-stop after a real block correctly re-acquires the freed lock (test_agent_lock_is_released_after_a_blocked_stop passes; the lock file itself is deliberately left on disk rather than unlinked, specifically so a racing process cannot take a flock on a different inode of the same name). An unwritable .agent-locks parent fails closed with a named PermissionError, leaving the receipt 'open' and no ledger row written (test_agent_lock_directory_failure_is_fail_closed passes). A planted symlink AT THE LOCK FILE itself is refused via O_NOFOLLOW -> ELOOP, not silently redirected (test_planted_symlink_at_the_agent_lock_path_blocks passes). LOCK_NB makes every acquisition a try-lock (fails immediately, never blocks), so hold-and-wait deadlock is impossible by construction, and the lock/claim acquisition order is fixed and one-way. All held across the whole guarded region via try/finally, so a crash or any of the ~20 block();return paths inside consume_under_agent_lock still releases it on process exit (kernel-released flock) or on `finally: os.close(lock_fd)`.
evidence_refs: .agent-harness/tests/test_hooks.py#L3561-L3665 (the four shipped lock fixtures, confirmed passing)

findings.statement: COVERAGE GAP, not a live bypass: acquire_agent_lock's `directory.is_symlink()` guard (protects against `.agent-harness/admissions/<run>/.agent-locks/` itself, as opposed to the lock FILE, being a planted symlink) is load-bearing and CURRENTLY CORRECT -- I built a fresh PoC (test_r7_symlinked_agent_lock_directory_itself_is_blocked) that plants `.agent-locks` as a symlink to an outside directory before a legitimate stop, and the real hook correctly blocks with 'the agent lock directory is a symlink', leaves the receipt open, writes nothing through the symlink, and appends no ledger row -- but mutation-testing shows this exact guard has ZERO regression-test coverage in the shipped 102-fixture suite: replacing `if directory.is_symlink():` with `if False:` in the sandbox's real subagent_stop_validate.py left all 102 tests green. This matters because O_NOFOLLOW on `os.open(lock_file, ...)` only protects the FINAL path component; it does not stop traversal through a symlinked PARENT directory, so this specific check is the only thing standing between a planted `.agent-locks` symlink and the lock being silently taken on an attacker-chosen inode outside the repo (defeating the mutual exclusion the round-6 fix exists to provide). The shipped suite already has an analogous, correctly-covered test for the LOCK FILE being a symlink (test_planted_symlink_at_the_agent_lock_path_blocks); this is its untested sibling for the DIRECTORY. Planting the symlink itself still requires the same-OS-user residual (unrestricted repo write), so this is not an exploit of the current bytes -- it is a hole in the regression net that would let a future edit silently reopen the case without any of the 102 tests noticing.
assumptions_used: A guard clause with a real, currently-correct effect but zero fixture coverage is reported as a 'fail' against the claim 'the newest fixtures adequately protect the newest security-relevant code' (what round 7 was asked to test), not as a claim that the current bytes are exploitable -- they are not, per my own passing PoC.

counterevidence_refs: My own PoC proves the current, unmutated code blocks this scenario correctly, so no live bypass exists in the bytes at cef6f00.

findings.statement: COVERAGE GAP, not a live bypass, and lower-impact than F-R7-02 due to defense-in-depth: admit_agent.py's own `open_chain_started_at` (which decides what THIS SCRIPT stamps as created_at/chain_started_at on a new receipt and ledger row) has an `and not started` accumulation guard whose only real purpose is to keep a SECOND, real, consecutive minted/reopened ledger row (no intervening consume) from moving the chain start forward. Mutation-testing shows zero fixture in the shipped 102-suite exercises this: deleting the guard (`elif event in (...) and not started:` -> `elif event in (...):`) left all 102 tests green. Every shipped 'nested reopen' fixture (test_nested_reopen_separates_chain_age_from_supersession, test_reopening_a_never_consumed_receipt_carries_the_chain_start_forward) uses the `_backdate_open_chain` helper to directly edit the ledger's existing row IN PLACE between CLI calls, which collapses the ledger back down to exactly one relevant row before each read -- so no shipped fixture ever makes admit_agent.py read TWO real, un-backdated minted/reopened rows in one call. I confirmed via a direct unit-level test (test_r7_chain_start_ignores_a_second_consecutive_open_mint_row, calling the real function against a hand-built two-row ledger) that the CURRENT code is correct: both admit_agent.open_chain_started_at and its independent twin validate_harness.open_admission_chain_start return the FIRST row's timestamp, not the second's. The twin in validate_harness.py IS separately protected by test_reopen_does_not_restart_the_in_flight_ceiling (confirmed: mutating ITS gate the same way is caught, because that fixture happens to leave two real rows in the ledger before the validator's own read). Severity is low rather than medium because even a silent future regression of admit_agent.py's copy alone would not defeat the actual enforcement: pending_carve_out_refusal in validate_harness.py always recomputes chain age from the raw, always-accurate `at` field on each ledger row directly, never trusting the receipt's or ledger row's own `chain_started_at` field -- exactly per the code comment 'validate_harness.py reconstructs this from the append-only rows regardless -- that stays the authority, this field does not replace it.' So a regression here would produce a misleading created_at/chain_started_at DISPLAY value and a misleading warning message, not a bypassed ceiling.
assumptions_used: Impact is scoped by reading the actual consumer of chain_started_at (pending_carve_out_refusal), which is confirmed to ignore the receipt/ledger-row field entirely and recompute from raw `at` timestamps; this is a source-level fact, not an inference.

findings.statement: CONFIRMED behavioural property, empirically reproduced, characterised as an intentional-but-broad-blast-radius side effect rather than an accidental defect: merge_results.py's new attribution gate (importing validate_harness.collect_result_attribution, per the round-6 docstring's stated goal of 'one shared pass, so the merge gate and the validator cannot disagree') couples merging the ACTIVE run's genuinely-attributed, cleanly-admitted results to the health of EVERY OTHER run directory under .agent-harness/runs/ -- including old, archived, non-active runs that predate this scheme entirely. Reproduced directly: with a fully admitted, mergeable active-run result already merging cleanly, adding a second, unrelated, non-active, archived run directory whose ADMISSIONS.jsonl contains one malformed line causes merge_results.py to refuse the ACTIVE run's merge entirely ('attribution: Malformed admission ledger line: ...'), leaving MERGED_RESULTS.json untouched. This coupling is genuinely NEW for merge_results.py specifically: the pre-round-6 script had no ledger/attribution gating at all and would have merged the active run's results regardless of any other run's state. validate_harness.py itself already had this exact global blast radius before round 6 (confirmed: the same corruption already fails validate_harness.py's own 'ok' verdict on the pre-round-6 loop structure too, since it iterates run_dirs(harness) unconditionally), so this is not a new hole in validate_harness.py, only a newly-inherited one in merge_results.py. Given the D-070 admission binding report records roughly 83 run directories accumulated so far, and merge is meant to be the operator step that produces the artifact the adjudicator reads, any corruption anywhere in that growing history -- including pre-dating the receipt/ledger scheme -- can silently block every future merge. It fails SAFE (refuses rather than merging unvetted bytes) rather than open, which is the correct direction for a security-relevant gate, so this is reported as an operational/availability risk for the D-070 adjudicator to weigh, not as a bypass.
assumptions_used: Failing safe (refusing to merge) rather than open (merging anyway) is the correct direction for a security gate, so this finding is reported as an operational-risk characterisation rather than a bypass, matching how the assignment distinguishes a wedge/DoS concern from an actual security hole.

findings.statement: REFUTED as an accidental regression, CONFIRMED as deliberate, disclosed, already-tested design: a malformed ADMISSIONS.jsonl line in the active run's ledger does hard-fail 'Hook preflight: FAIL' for EVERY never-minted agent_id in that run, not only the one default fixture agent -- I verified this directly against three distinct, unrelated agent_ids (agent-helper-alpha/beta/gamma), all FAILed by the same single corrupt line. This matches the assignment's named DoS concern exactly, but it is not new or accidental: the shipped fixture test_subagentstart_fails_on_a_malformed_admission_ledger_line already asserts this exact behaviour is CORRECT for its one agent, the module docstring states the rule explicitly ('an unprovable negative must not default to PASS. Ambiguity is a FAIL, not a skip'), and the failure is advisory only -- SubagentStart in this harness architecture cannot mechanically block a spawn; it only injects context instructing the agent to stop substantive work and report an error. The actual security gate (the admission receipt/token check) lives at Stop and is entirely unaffected by this: it does not consult the ledger for agent_ids it was never told to check. So this is a real, broad, but intentional fail-safe trade-off (every helper agent in a run with a corrupted ledger is told to stand down) rather than a bypass or an accidental hole.

findings.statement: REFUTED: check_one_agent_one_assignment does not false-positive on any real ledger shape I could construct, including all three named in the assignment. A legitimate declared release (reopen naming the correct agent_id in superseded_consumed_by_agent_id, with a non-empty reason, for the assignment that agent actually holds) correctly clears the binding and lets the same agent legitimately bind elsewhere -- covered by the shipped test_check_one_agent_one_assignment_over_ledger_row_sequences's 'a declared release rebinds the same agent' clean case. A resumed agent re-consuming the SAME assignment twice produces no error -- 'the same agent re-consuming the same assignment' clean case in the same test (and this matches reality: subagent_stop_validate.py's idempotent re-stop path returns without writing a second ledger 'consumed' row at all, so this shape does not even normally arise). --agent-id-unknown (token-only) receipts do not false-positive either: the shipped test_concurrent_stops_by_distinct_agents_are_both_admitted mints two assignments --agent-id-unknown and has two DIFFERENT real agent_ids consume them concurrently over many trials, all cleanly admitted with no wedge -- and by inspection check_one_agent_one_assignment never reads expected_agent_id or agent_binding at all, only the real, Stop-recorded agent_id on each 'consumed' row, so token-only minting cannot affect this check's verdict either way.

None of the 102 shipped fixtures were found to be vacuous in the sense of passing regardless of the code under test; the gap in both surviving cases is an ABSENT fixture for a real code path, not a present-but-useless one.

findings.statement: NOT TESTABLE in this environment, reviewed by code inspection only: NFS-style environments where flock() semantics differ from local POSIX filesystems. acquire_agent_lock's failure handling distinguishes only BlockingIOError (treated as 'another stop holds it, retry') from every other OSError (treated as fail-closed, block). Some real-world NFS configurations (older NFSv3 without a running lockd/statd, or certain network/overlay filesystems) do not raise EITHER exception on fcntl.flock -- they silently succeed regardless of contention, because the kernel or the filesystem driver has no cross-client locking to enforce. In that specific configuration, this code would not hit ANY of its error paths at all; it would believe it acquired an exclusive lock while providing none, which is a silent fail-OPEN rather than the fail-closed behaviour every other failure mode in this function deliberately chooses. This could not be reproduced or refuted in this sandbox (a single local ext4 filesystem, single OS user, no NFS mount available), and does not apply to the recorded LOCAL-ADAPT deployment (VS Code, single OS user, hooks invoked explicitly, no network filesystem in play) -- but it is a real, named limitation of flock as the chosen primitive that the module docstring's design rationale ('the kernel releases it... structurally') does not account for, and is recorded here rather than silently passed over, per the assignment's explicit ask.
assumptions_used: General knowledge of flock-over-NFS behaviour on some historical/misconfigured NFS setups is cited as a documented characteristic of the primitive, not verified against this specific host (no NFS mount was available to test against).
evidence_refs: .codex/hooks/subagent_stop_validate.py#L108-L127 (acquire_agent_lock's exception handling: BlockingIOError vs generic OSError, with no third path for a silent no-op)
counterevidence_refs: The recorded deployment (LOCAL-ADAPT: single OS user, VS Code invoking hooks explicitly, no network filesystem) does not exercise this path, so it is not applicable to current operation -- recorded as a residual limitation of the chosen primitive, not a defect in the shipped bytes for this deployment.
unresolved: Whether this deployment will ever run its .agent-harness tree on a network filesystem is unknown to this reviewer; if it will not, this finding is purely documentary.

findings.statement: REFUTED: the anywhere-sweep token detector is exact, not heuristic, and I found no false positive or false negative in direct testing. find_candidate_tokens windows every maximal run of the token alphabet at every offset and at lengths within +/-2 of the real, runtime-derived TOKEN_BYTES-implied length, but a candidate is only ever REPORTED or REWRITTEN if its sha256 exactly matches a KNOWN receipt's token_digest read live off disk (collect_known_token_digests) -- an ordinary base64-ish string of the same length and alphabet, with no matching digest, is never flagged, confirmed with a same-length decoy planted next to a real leaked token in my incident-reproduction smoke test (only the real token was reported). Re-attack of the previously-closed items in this file (ledger-pinned bytes refusing a silent rewrite that would invalidate a validator-trusted digest; idempotent already-scrubbed values; escaped/non-JSON evidence) found no change: the shipped test_scrub_admission_proof_replaces_token_with_digest and test_scrubber_reaches_escaped_and_non_json_evidence both still pass and this round's diff does not touch the original field-scrub code path at all (git diff confirms the additions are strictly additive: new functions plus a new --sweep/--verify-result/--sweep-run dispatch in main(), with the original scrub()/cmd behaviour for the field-scrub path unchanged).
assumptions_used: A token deliberately fragmented by inserting a non-alphabet character mid-token (not exercised by the actual incident, which was an ordinary contiguous paste) would be missed by design, since the detector only windows CONTIGUOUS alphabet runs; this is a known, narrow scope limitation stated in the module's own docstring's method description, not a defect found by this review.

findings.statement: CONFIRMED, independently reproduced against the actual committed cef6f00 bytes in my isolated sandbox (not copied from any other source -- see the 'commands' entry noting a concurrent, unrelated, uncommitted edit I incidentally observed in the real repo mid-session, which I did not read for its conclusions before building my own reproduction from scratch): describe_admission_receipt in subagent_start_context.py only consults the round-6 ledger-based orphaned-mint check inside `if not matches:` -- i.e. only when the agent_id has ZERO receipt files anywhere in the run. One healthy, valid, open, right-run receipt for ANY assignment therefore silences the check for every OTHER assignment the same agent_id might also be orphaned on. Reproduced end to end with the real CLI and the real hook: minted assignment A for agent-g with the admissions dir chmod 0500 (receipt write fails, ledger append succeeds -- a genuine orphaned mint, confirmed via the ledger row and the absent receipt file), then minted assignment B for the SAME agent-g normally (a real, healthy, open receipt). The real SubagentStart hook for agent-g then reports `Admission receipt: open, bound to assignment 'A-HOOK-FIXTURE-2'` and `Hook preflight: PASS`, with no mention of the orphaned assignment A at all. This is exactly the composite shape round 6's own module docstring claims is now a hard FAIL ('a minted row naming this agent_id with no receipt on disk is a failed mint, and Start can read it... the obligation-2 case, and it is now enforced rather than argued away') -- the claim holds only when the agent has no OTHER receipt, which is not stated as a qualification anywhere in the round-6 docstring's three-state model. Impact is bounded the same way as F-R7-06: Start's preflight verdict is advisory only (it cannot mechanically block a spawn, and per round 6's own F-R6-14, subagent_start_preflight is self-attested by the agent and never cross-checked against real Start output), and Stop's actual security gate is unaffected -- if agent-g later tried to submit a HARNESS_RESULT for the orphaned assignment A, Stop would refuse it regardless (no receipt file exists for A to validate against). So no live security bypass results, but the round-6 fix's own headline claim for this exact composite case does not hold as stated, which is precisely the class of gap this whole review chain exists to catch.
assumptions_used: Independence from the concurrently-observed, uncommitted third-party edit: I constructed and ran this reproduction myself, from the assignment's own description of round 6's stated three-state model, against my own isolated sandbox's committed bytes, before forming a conclusion -- the concurrent edit is noted for transparency (per 'report every attack... whether it succeeded'), not relied upon as evidence.

Neither of the two shipped fixtures nearest this code (test_subagentstart_hard_fails_on_an_orphaned_mint, test_subagentstart_passes_for_an_unregistered_agent_despite_ledger_activity) constructs an agent that holds BOTH a healthy receipt for one assignment AND an orphaned mint for another; both mint only one assignment total in their fixture, so neither could have caught this.
